subtitle: Early network experiments connecting MIT to Multics and Harvard

tldr.problem: MIT wanted to demonstrate that the early ARPANET could support practical remote terminal access and run programs on remote systems, not just send messages.
tldr.mechanism: Using a simplified interim NCP (IINCP) that handled raw IMP messages, MIT connected its MITDG PDP-10 system to Multics, then to Harvard's PDP-10, and finally executed graphics programs remotely at MIT's Evans & Sutherland display system using programs received from Harvard.
tldr.outcome: These experiments showed that networked computing was feasible and identified issues like control character mismatches between systems and the challenges of terminal multiplexing across machines.

facts.label: Systems connected
facts.value: MITDG, Multics, Harvard PDP-10, Evans & Sutherland

today: RFC 89 documents the ARPANET's transition from experimental protocol to a practical tool for remote computing. The issues it describes (control character translation, terminal emulation, flow control) remain relevant to modern remote work, though now handled by terminal emulation software and SSH rather than custom NCP code. The graphics experiment foreshadowed cloud computing and distributed processing.

sections.title: Early Remote Access Experiments
sections.content: In January 1971, Bob Metcalfe and colleagues at MIT described three historic experiments using an interim interim NCP (IINCP) on their MITDG PDP-6/10 system. Rather than waiting for the full Network Control Program, they wrote programs that spoke directly to the IMP hardware, allowing them to achieve milestones: connecting an MITDG terminal to Multics, connecting to Harvard's PDP-10, and executing graphics programs remotely across the network. The IINCP approach taught them about flow control and the ARPANET's protocol details.
sections.eli5: MIT built a quick network system without waiting for the official one, and used it to connect their computers to computers at other universities.

sections.title: Multics and Harvard Connections
sections.content: Connecting MITDG to Multics revealed challenges: Multics expected line-oriented half-duplex input (each character echoed), while MITDG was character-oriented. The team fixed the QUIT and RUBOUT characters and worked around Multics queuing issues. Connecting to Harvard exposed control character mismatches: Harvard's DEC system used control-C for QUIT and control-Z for EOF, while MIT's ITS system reversed them. This mismatch accidentally made remote work easier, but revealed the complexity of terminal protocol translation.
sections.eli5: Different computers had different keyboard rules. Control-C meant 'stop' on one system but 'end of file' on another. Getting remote terminals to work meant fixing these mismatches.

sections.title: Remote Graphics Processing
sections.content: The most ambitious experiment transmitted a complete PDP-10 core image containing a graphics program from Harvard, MIT received and loaded it, executed it with the Evans & Sutherland line drawing system, and sent the 2D display data back to Harvard for a PDP-1 to show. The protocol involved transmitting word count and starting address first, then allowing the program to run and specify result locations. Despite going through two time-sharing systems and three IMPs in series, response time was acceptably fast.
sections.eli5: Harvard sent a graphics program through the network to MIT, MIT ran it on its fancy graphics computer, and sent the result back to Harvard to display. It worked surprisingly fast.
